'''Myrta Blanca Silva Oliveros''' (September 11, 1927 – December 2, 1987) better known as '''Myrta Silva''', was a Puerto Rican singer, songwriter and television producer who was known affectionately as '''"La Gorda de Oro"'''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Myrta Silva: la "Gordita de Oro"|url=https://www.primerahora.com/entretenimiento/musica/notas/myrta-silva-la-gordita-de-oro/|website=Primera Hora|date=18 August 2012|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Biography of Myrta Silva (1923-1987)|url=http://thebiography.us/en/silva-myrta|last1=TheBiography.us|last2=TheBiography.us|website=thebiography.us|language=en|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Myrta Silva|url=http://www.proyectosalonhogar.com/Enciclopedia_Ilustrada/Myrta_Silva.htm|website=www.proyectosalonhogar.com|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> She rose to fame in 1949 as the lead vocalist for the Cuban ensemble [[Sonora Matancera]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|last=Zaleski|first=Tomasz|date=2003-07-18|title=Obituary: Celia Cruz|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2003/jul/18/guardianobituaries.arts|access-date=2020-05-07|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

==Early years==
Myrta Blanca Silva Oliveros<ref>{{Cite web|title=Myrta Silva|url=https://www.discogs.com/artist/1860232-Myrta-Silva|website=Discogs|language=en|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=MYRTA SILVA • Página Principal|url=https://www.cancioneros.com/at/394/0/biografia-de-myrta-silva|website=CANCIONEROS.COM|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> was born in the city of [[Arecibo, Puerto Rico]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Myrta Silva - Caribbean {{!}} EnciclopediaPR|url=https://enciclopediapr.org/en/encyclopedia/myrta-silva/|language=en-US|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> Her father died when she was six years old and she was raised by her mother, who was her inspiration. Silva and her fans referred to her mother as "Mama Yeya." In 1937, Silva made her first public presentation at the Oliver Theater in [[Arecibo]]. In these early years of her music career, she worked an average of twenty-five revue shows a week to support herself.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fiol-Matta |first=Licia |title=The great woman singer: gender and voice in Puerto Rican music |date=2017 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-6293-7 |series=Refiguring American music |location=Durham}}</ref> 

Circa 1938,<ref name=":1" /> Silva and her mother moved to New York, where she started a career in radio, theater and musical plays.<ref name="FNCP">{{Cite web|url=https://prpop.org/biografias/myrta-silva/|title=Myrta Silva|publisher=[[National Foundation for Popular Culture]]|location=San Juan, Puerto Rico|language=es}}</ref> In 1939, she made her debut in Brooklyn at the Atlantic Theater, soon becoming a regular at venues like the Teatro Hispano, [[Teatro Puerto Rico]], and [[Carnegie Hall]] in New York.

==Singing career==
Silva was working in a cabaret when she was discovered and offered a 10-year contract by [[RCA]]. In the late 1930s, she met the [[Puerto Rico|Puerto Rican]] composer [[Rafael Hernández Marín|Rafael Hernández]], who convinced her to join his Cuarteto Victoria.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fiol-Matta |first=Licia |title=The great woman singer: gender and voice in Puerto Rican music |date=2017 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-6282-1 |series=Refiguring American music |location=Durham}}</ref> Myrta traveled with the group all over [[Latin-America]]. Some time later, she also sang for another composer [[Pedro Flores (composer)|Pedro Flores]] in his Sexteto Flores, where she was joined by [[Daniel Santos (singer)|Daniel Santos]] and [[Pedro Ortiz Dávila]].<ref name="MOPR">[http://www.musicofpuertorico.com/index.php/artists/myrta_silva Music of Puerto Rico]</ref>

===As a composer===
{{External media

| audio1  = You may listen to {{YouTube|AeFMT_2ai6E|Awilda Pedroza's interpretation of Silvas "Qué sabes tú?"}}.
| audio2  = and to [[Luciano Quiñones]] piano interpretation [http://www.piano-bar.com/pages/sabestu.htm here]

In 1941, aged 14, Silva composed her first song, "Cuando Vuelvas" ("When You Return"), recorded by [[Ruth Fernández]]. In 1942, she composed "En Mi Soledad" ("In My Solitude"), recorded by Daniel Santos, which became a hit in Latin America and in the Latin communities in the United States. Silva became the first woman certified as a ''timbalera'' by the [[American Federation of Musicians|American Federation of Music]] in 1943.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fiol-Matta |first=Licia |title=The great woman singer: gender and voice in Puerto Rican music |date=2017 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-6282-1 |series=Refiguring American music |location=Durham}}</ref> In 1944, she wrote "Asi es la Vida" ("That's Life") and "Facil de Recordar" ("Easy to Remember") while she was performing in [[Havana, Cuba]].<ref name="FNCP"/>

Silva had become an international singing star and was known as "The Queen of the Guaracha" by her fans in Latin America. From 1949 to 1950, she was the lead singer in the popular Cuban ensemble, [[La Sonora Matancera]], at the same time continuing to compose. She received a good deal of recognition for her groups' performances throughout Latin America. In [[Argentina]], she was named the "best-selling artist" in that country. In 1950, she was proclaimed by the Cuban government "The Most Popular Artist." When she decided to leave the group she was replaced by [[Celia Cruz]], a young school teacher turned singer who went on to become known as the "Queen of Salsa."<ref name=":0" />

===Madame Chencha===
In the 1950s, together with the Cuban composer [[Ñico Saquito]] (Antonio Fernández), Silva wrote a humorous song titled “Camina Como Chencha” (“Walk Like Chencha”).<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Fiol-Matta|first=Licia|date=2008-11-01|title=Chencha's gait|journal=Women & Performance: A Journal of Feminist Theory|volume=18|issue=3|pages=287–301|doi=10.1080/07407700802496041|s2cid=191345386|issn=0740-770X}}</ref> In 1956, Silva produced and transmitted from New York a television program, ''Una Hora Contigo'' (''An Hour with You''). The show was transmitted by Canal 4 in Puerto Rico and Myrta moved back to the island. In her show she re-created the innovative character of "Madame Chencha." "Madame Chencha" became the first [[T.V.]] character dedicated to "rumors."<ref>In this connection, see [[Rita Montaner#Rita la Chismosa]]</ref> This character created a lot of controversy between public figures and the television station, and as a consequence, Silva decided to leave the program and return to New York City.<ref name="FNCP"/>

===In New York City===
In New York City, she composed "Puerto Rico del Alma" ("Puerto Rico of my Soul"). Between 1962 and 1964, she composed the following hit songs: "Que Sabes Tu" ("What do you know?"), "Tengo que Acostumbrarme" ("I Have To Get Used To It"), "Juguetes del Destino" ("Toys of Destiny"), and many others.<ref name="MOPR"/> Among her recordings are ''Voces Romanticas de Puerto Rico'' (Romantic voices of Puerto Rico), ''La Bombonera de San Juan'' (The Bombonera of San Juan) and ''La Compositora E interprete'' (The Composer and Interpreter).

===''Una Hora Contigo'' (''An Hour with You'')===
During the mid 1960s, Silva hosted a weekly music variety TV show ''Una Hora Contigo'' (''An Hour with You'') on New York City's first Spanish language television station, WNJU-TV Channel 47. The program was hugely popular among the Latino audience, prompting the station to add an additional weekly program hosted by Silva titled ''Tira y Tapate''.

In the 1970s, Silva wrote "No Te Vayas de Mi Vida" ("Stay In My Life") which was recorded and made popular by [[Evelyn Souffront]]. 

In 1971, Silva returned to Puerto Rico with her television show ''Una Hora Contigo'' which this time was transmitted on Canal 11. This show was among the most popular programs in Puerto Rico.<ref name="MOPR" />

==Later years==
Silva was active in many charities and she also participated in many pro-Hispanic activities in the US. During the 1980s, Silva had a program in the government television channel dedicated to music and composers. In 2016, Myrta Silva was inducted into the [[Latin Songwriters Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latinsonghall.com/about-us/inductees/2016-inductees/|title = 2016 Inductees – Latin Songwriters Hall of Fame}}</ref>

Silva suffered from [[dementia]] in her last years. One day while showering, she accidentally scalded herself with the hot water and suffered third degree burns. Silva died on December 2, 1987, in Arecibo, aged 60 and was buried in [[Santa María Magdalena de Pazzis Cemetery]] in [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]].
